name: Khor Fakkan
title: Khor Fakkan Thickness Gauging | Container Ships and Bunker Calls
description: Ultrasonic thickness gauging at Khor Fakkan for mainline container ships, feeders and tankers at anchor: hull, ballast tanks, hatch coamings and scrubber lines.
h1: Hull and Tank Thickness Measurement at Khor Fakkan on the Gulf of Oman
intro: Khor Fakkan, Sharjah's town on the Gulf of Oman coast, has one of the few natural deep-water harbours in the UAE and a container terminal that serves the country without a passage through the Strait of Hormuz. Mainline container ships, Gulf feeders and the tankers and bulk carriers waiting or bunkering at the anchorage offshore all pass close by. No Atlantis staff live on this coast; technicians travel from India for each vessel and reach it alongside or by launch.

ballast tank gauging gulf of oman

highlights.p: The terminal receives some of the largest container ships in service as well as the feeders that connect it with the Gulf, Iraq, the Indian subcontinent and East Africa. Calls by the big ships are brief, so deck, coaming and ballast tank readings are ranked to fit them.

highlights.h: Bunker and waiting calls at anchor
highlights.p: High-sulphur fuel oil is supplied to ships at the Khor Fakkan anchorage from storage tankers and barges, drawing scrubber-fitted ships and tankers that may lie offshore for a day or more. That time suits wash-water piping checks and work in ballast tanks the crew has prepared.

From late spring to early autumn, deck and tank temperatures on the east coast are extreme and the humidity is high. Work in enclosed spaces is planned for the cooler hours, with ventilation, rest periods and water agreed with the master, so readings in double bottoms and wing tanks are taken safely.

port.h: A deep harbour under the Hajar mountains, the terminal and the anchorage
p: Khor Fakkan lies on a bay on the UAE's east coast, part of the emirate of Sharjah but cut off from the city of Sharjah by the Hajar mountains, with Fujairah to the south and Dibba and the Omani border further north. The bay's deep water close inshore made it a natural harbour, and a road through the mountains, with long tunnels, links the town and port with Sharjah and the rest of the UAE's Gulf coast. Ships approach from the Gulf of Oman, the open sea that carries traffic to and from the Strait of Hormuz, and the port lies only a short distance off that main route, so ships can call or stop offshore without a detour through the strait. Tides are modest and the sea is usually calm, though occasional strong winds can raise enough sea to interrupt launch transfers.

The terminal is run by Gulftainer, which has operated it for decades and has been expanding its capacity and its inland links, including bonded dry ports at Sajaa and Al Dhaid that let cargo landed at Khor Fakkan move inland to the emirate's logistics zones. Mainline container services from Asia, the Mediterranean and beyond call here alongside feeder ships that redistribute boxes to the Gulf ports, Iraq, Pakistan, India and East Africa, and the terminal has handled container ships of the largest class now trading. Because it can work both as a transhipment hub and as a gateway for UAE imports, its traffic rises whenever routing through the strait becomes harder and eases again when conditions settle. A planned Etihad Rail connection is expected to add a rail route inland.

Offshore, the Khor Fakkan anchorage shares the east-coast waiting waters with Fujairah, and ships stop there for bunkers, stores, crew changes, orders and berth windows. In recent years it has grown into a supply point for high-sulphur fuel oil, held in floating storage nearby and transferred ship-to-ship into bunker barges for delivery, and the barge fleet working this coast has grown with it. The Sharjah and Fujairah port authorities have issued notices restricting where ships may anchor off this coast, and ships found anchored in restricted areas have faced sanctions, so the agent confirms the anchorage position before arrival. Summer brings very high air and sea temperatures and heavy humidity, while the cooler months from November to March are the easiest for work on deck and in tanks.

facilities.h: Where a ship can be gauged at Khor Fakkan
p: Container ships are gauged alongside at the terminal during their call. A mainline ship may work for a day or so and a feeder for less, so the team concentrates on hatch coamings, deck plating near the hatch corners, lashing bridges, cross-deck structure and the ballast tanks the ship can release, working around crane lanes and lashing gangs under the terminal's safety rules. Scrubber-fitted ships can have their wash-water and overboard piping measured from the engine room and scrubber spaces while cargo work goes on above. The agent obtains the gate passes and boarding clearance for the terminal.

At the anchorage, tankers, bulk carriers and container ships waiting or taking bunkers are reached by a launch booked through the agent. The anchorage suits planned work in ballast tanks, void spaces and the pump room, with cargo tanks added only once they have been cleaned, gas-freed and certified for entry. Khor Fakkan has no dry dock for merchant ships; ships needing a docking go to the large yards in Dubai, at Duqm in Oman or further afield, so readings taken here usually travel ahead to the yard as a pre-docking steel estimate. Bunker barges and supply craft working the anchorage are gauged at their lay-by berths between jobs when the port allows.

Scrubber spaces on container ships alongside — wash-water supply, discharge and overboard piping measured while cargo work continues
Khor Fakkan anchorage — ballast tank, void and pump room work on tankers and bulk carriers waiting or bunkering, reached by launch

context.h: Port state control, the bunker market and trading conditions off the east coast
p: The UAE takes part in port state control under the Riyadh MoU, and foreign ships calling at Khor Fakkan, or stopping offshore for bunkers and services, fall within its reach. The fuel trade at the anchorage brings scrutiny of its own: owners and charterers with strict compliance policies check the origin of fuel bought on this coast carefully. The ships buying high-sulphur fuel here, mostly scrubber-fitted bulk carriers, tankers and container ships, depend on scrubber systems whose wash-water and discharge lines suffer fast corrosion and erosion. Measuring those lines during a bunker stop gives the owner early warning before a leak through the shell or a failed overboard connection takes the scrubber out of service and forces a change of fuel.

Trading patterns matter too. Feeder ships based on the UAE coast shuttle between Khor Fakkan, Jebel Ali and the smaller Gulf ports, and on to Iraq, Pakistan and India, with short passages in warm, salty water and almost no time out of service, so ballast tank coatings and seawater cooling lines age quickly. Mainline container ships calling here are generally younger, but their hatch corners, coaming ends and lashing bridges develop fatigue cracks that magnetic particle and dye penetrant checks find before they spread. Tankers at the anchorage include ships on Gulf crude and product trades whose decks and cargo-tank tops endure intense heat for much of the year, and the older ones among them face vetting and charterer questions that measured condition data helps to answer.

jobs.h: Gauging jobs we see at Khor Fakkan
jobs.p: Work at Khor Fakkan follows the ship's reason for stopping. Container ships alongside give a short, predictable window for focused deck, coaming and tank scopes; ships at anchor give a longer but less certain one, which can end without notice when a berth, a cargo or new orders arrive. We agree a ranked compartment list with the superintendent before the team travels, prepare the TM plan from the ship's drawings, and report readings at the end of each day so that partial results are still useful if the ship sails early. Heat is planned for: in summer, enclosed-space work starts early, runs with forced ventilation and rest breaks, and pauses in the hottest hours when tank temperatures make safe work impossible.

Scrubber wash-water and overboard pipe gauging on a bulk carrier taking high-sulphur fuel at the anchorage.
Ballast tank and seawater cooling pipe gauging on a Gulf container feeder ahead of its renewal survey at a Dubai yard.
Pre-purchase inspection of a product tanker waiting off Khor Fakkan, sampling deck, ballast tanks and cargo-tank deckheads for a buyer.
Condition gauging of a bunker barge's hull and cargo tanks at its lay-by berth between supply runs.

logistics: Sharjah International Airport and Dubai International Airport both have frequent direct flights from India, and Fujairah International Airport is closer to the east coast; from the Gulf-side airports the team drives through the mountains to Khor Fakkan. UAE visas for the team are arranged before travel, so we ask for the ship's dates as soon as they are known. The ship's agent obtains terminal gate passes and, for anchorage jobs, books the launch and any marine permits needed for boarding.
vessels: Bunker barges and floating storage tankers

faqs.q: Can a container ship be gauged during a short call at Khor Fakkan?
faqs.a: Yes, with a focused scope. Hatch coamings, deck plating near the hatch corners, lashing bridges and a selection of ballast tanks can be covered in a day if the ship prepares the tanks before arrival and the agent has the passes ready. Larger programmes, such as a full renewal survey set, are better split across calls or completed in dock, with the Khor Fakkan readings forming the first part of the report.

faqs.q: Is anchorage work possible while a ship takes bunkers off Khor Fakkan?
faqs.a: Often, but bunkering comes first. Fuel transfer ties up the deck crew and restricts movement near the manifold and bunker stations, so tank entry and deck work are scheduled around it with the chief engineer and chief officer. Scrubber piping in the engine room can usually be measured during the transfer. The launch, boarding time and any permits are arranged by the agent.

faqs.q: How do you manage summer heat in enclosed spaces?
faqs.a: By planning around it. Tanks are ventilated well before entry, atmosphere checks and permits follow the ship's procedures, and work is scheduled for the early morning and evening when temperatures inside double bottoms and wing tanks are lower. Rest breaks, water and a standby person at the entrance are agreed with the master. If a space is too hot to enter safely, it moves later in the plan.

faqs.q: Where do ships calling at Khor Fakkan go for dry docking?
faqs.a: There is no dry dock for merchant ships at Khor Fakkan itself. Ships usually dock at the large repair yards in Dubai, at Duqm in Oman, or in Bahrain and Asia. Gauging done at Khor Fakkan before the docking lets the yard plan steel renewal and order plate in advance, and the readings are located on the ship's drawings so the yard can use them without re-measuring everything.
